title: Phlebotomy, IV Access & Specimens
summary: Drawing blood that the lab will actually run: the right patient, the right tube in the right order, a clean stick, uncontaminated cultures, working IV access, and specimens that survive the trip to the lab.

lessons.title: The right patient, the right label
lessons.body:
## The error that kills quietly

Everything else in this module is technique. This lesson is about the one mistake that kills people who were never even sick from the thing that was treated.

A mislabeled specimen means a result attached to the wrong human being. Someone gets a potassium that belongs to another patient, or a blood type that belongs to another patient, and then gets treated for it. Transfusing the wrong blood type causes a hemolytic reaction that can kill in minutes, and the root cause is nearly always a labeling error at the bedside, not a laboratory error.

The Joint Commission lists wrong-patient identification among its National Patient Safety Goals, and a mislabeled blood bank specimen is treated as a serious reportable event in most hospitals.

> **Key:** The specimen is only as good as the name on it. A perfect draw on the wrong patient is worse than no draw at all, because it produces a confident wrong answer.

## Two identifiers, and the word active

Use **two patient identifiers**, neither of which is the room number or bed location. The standard pair is full name and date of birth, matched against the wristband and the requisition or label.

Ask **actively**, not passively.

- Passive (wrong): Are you Robert Klein? A confused, hard-of-hearing, sedated or simply polite patient says yes to anything.
- Active (right): Tell me your full name and date of birth.

Then compare what they said to the wristband, and compare the wristband to the labels in your hand. Three things must agree: the patient's spoken answer, the band, and the label.

If the patient cannot answer — unconscious, intubated, demented, a young child — use the wristband plus a second source: a family member at the bedside, or the identity confirmed by the nurse, per policy. An unidentified trauma patient carries a temporary identification number (a John Doe or Trauma Alpha band); that number is the identifier and it never comes off until a licensed process replaces it.

> **Trap:** Never draw on a patient with no wristband. Get the nurse to band the patient first. The five seconds you save is the entire safety system.

## Labeling at the bedside, in the patient's presence

Labels go on the tubes **at the bedside, immediately after the draw, before you leave the room, while the patient is still in front of you.**

- **Never pre-label** tubes before the draw. If the stick fails, or you get called away, or you move to another patient, you now have a labeled tube containing somebody else's blood or nothing at all.
- **Never carry unlabeled tubes** out of the room to label at a counter. Two technicians with handfuls of tubes at the same counter is the classic path to a fatal swap.

A complete label carries the patient's full name, a second identifier such as date of birth or medical record number, the date, the **exact time of collection**, and your initials or identification. Blood bank specimens carry additional requirements, usually a separate band with a unique number recorded on the tube.

The time matters more than people expect: troponin timing, drug levels, lactate clearance and blood alcohol are all interpreted against the collection time, not the time the lab received it.

> **On shift:** If you are ever unsure whether a tube is correctly labeled, throw it out and redraw. A second stick is an inconvenience. A wrong result is a treatment decision made on a fiction.
keyPoints: Mislabeled specimens produce confidently wrong results, and a mislabeled blood bank tube can kill through a transfusion reaction.
Use two identifiers, never the room or bed number: usually full name and date of birth.
Ask actively — tell me your name and date of birth — and match the answer, the wristband and the label.
Label at the bedside, after the draw, in the patient's presence. Never pre-label and never label at a counter.
The label carries name, second identifier, date, exact collection time, and your initials.

checks.q: Which is the correct way to identify a patient before a draw?
choices: Are you Mr. Klein in bed 4?
Tell me your full name and date of birth, then compare to the wristband and the labels
Check the room number against the requisition
Ask the nurse who is in the room
checks.why: Active identification with two identifiers is the standard, because a confused or polite patient will agree to any name offered. Room and bed number are explicitly not acceptable identifiers.

checks.q: When are tubes labeled?
choices: Before the draw, so nothing is forgotten
At the bedside immediately after the draw, with the patient present
At the counter outside the room, to keep the field clean
When the tubes reach the lab
checks.why: Pre-labeling produces a labeled tube with the wrong or no blood if the stick fails or you are interrupted. Labeling away from the bedside is how tubes from two patients get swapped.

checks.q: Why does the exact collection time matter on the label?
choices: It is only a billing requirement
Troponin, drug levels, lactate and alcohol are all interpreted against collection time, not receipt time
It determines which centrifuge is used
It sets the order of draw
checks.why: Serial and timed results depend on when the blood left the patient. A tube timed at lab receipt shifts the whole clinical picture and can cause a real result to be misread as rising or falling.

lessons.title: The order of draw, and why it exists
lessons.body:
## Additives travel backwards

Every blood collection tube contains a chemical: an anticoagulant, a clot activator, a gel, or a preservative. When the needle stays in the vein and tubes are changed on it, a tiny amount of the additive from the previous tube can carry back along the needle into the next one.

That carryover is invisible, it is measured in microliters, and it can completely change a result.

> **Key:** The order of draw is not tradition. It is a physical sequence that prevents chemical contamination between tubes, in order from least harmful contaminant to most.

## The order

1. **Blood culture bottles** (yellow SPS bottles or the culture set) — first, always. Cultures are drawn into a sterile bottle, and anything drawn before them risks introducing contamination into a sterile specimen.
2. **Light blue** — sodium citrate. Coagulation studies.
3. **Serum tubes** — red plain, and gold or red-grey SST with clot activator and gel.
4. **Green** — heparin (lithium or sodium).
5. **Lavender or pink** — EDTA.
6. **Gray** — sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate.

A common memory phrase runs: **Boys Love Ravishing Girls Like Grandma** — Blood culture, Light blue, Red or gold, Green, Lavender, Gray.

## What goes wrong when the order is broken

Two carryover errors matter enormously in an emergency department, and they are the reason anybody cares about this list.

**Lavender before anything else contaminates the next tube with EDTA and potassium.** The EDTA anticoagulant is a potassium salt (`K2EDTA` or `K3EDTA`). Carryover into a chemistry tube produces a **falsely high potassium** — sometimes wildly high, like `7.5` in a well patient — and a **falsely low calcium**, because EDTA binds calcium. The falsely high potassium is the single most common preventable cause of an emergency department phone call about a critical result on a patient who feels fine.

**Light blue drawn after a heparin tube gives falsely shortened clotting times**, and light blue drawn after a serum tube can pick up clot activator, falsely shortening the PT or aPTT. Coagulation results drive anticoagulant dosing, so the consequence is a real dose error.

The gray tube last is for the same reason in reverse: sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate poison many other assays, so it can contaminate nothing if nothing follows it.

## Two practical rules

**When light blue is the only tube ordered and you are using a straight needle**, no discard tube is needed. CLSI withdrew that requirement after studies disproved the old idea that tissue thromboplastin from the puncture meaningfully changes the PT or aPTT. A few laboratories still have their own policy; follow your own lab's policy.

**With a butterfly set and a light blue tube first**, always draw a discard tube first. The tubing of a butterfly holds roughly `0.5 mL` of air, and that air comes out of the vacuum of the first tube. In a light blue tube, which must be filled exactly to the line for the `9:1` blood-to-citrate ratio, the lost volume means an underfilled tube and a rejected specimen.

> **Trap:** The order applies to syringe transfers too, and it reverses your intuition: when filling tubes from a syringe you still fill in the same order — cultures, blue, serum, green, lavender, gray — because the risk is the needle carrying additive between tubes, not the direction of flow.

> **On shift:** When a critical potassium comes back on a patient who looks completely well, the first two questions are always the order of draw and whether the specimen was hemolyzed.
keyPoints: Order of draw prevents additive carryover between tubes: cultures, light blue, red or gold, green, lavender, gray.
EDTA (lavender) carryover falsely raises potassium and falsely lowers calcium — the classic cause of a critical potassium in a well patient.
Heparin or clot activator carried into light blue falsely shortens PT and aPTT, which drives anticoagulant dose errors.
With a butterfly, draw a discard tube first so tubing air does not underfill the light blue tube.
The same order applies when filling tubes from a syringe.

checks.q: Which tube is drawn first in a standard multi-tube draw?
choices: Light blue
Blood culture bottles
Gold SST
Lavender
checks.why: Blood cultures go first because they must stay sterile, and anything drawn before them risks contaminating the sterile bottle. Light blue is second, gray is last.

checks.q: A lavender tube was drawn before the chemistry tube. What result is most likely affected?
choices: A falsely high potassium and falsely low calcium
A falsely low glucose
A falsely high hemoglobin
A prolonged PT
checks.why: EDTA is a potassium salt that also binds calcium, so carryover raises potassium and lowers calcium. Glucose is affected by gray-tube preservatives, and PT by heparin or clot activator carryover.

checks.q: Why draw a discard tube first when using a butterfly set for a light blue tube?
choices: To warm the tubing
To check that the needle is in the vein
Because the tubing holds about 0.5 mL of air that would otherwise underfill the citrate tube
To reduce pain
checks.why: The butterfly tubing dead space consumes part of the first tube's vacuum with air. A light blue tube must be filled exactly to the line for the 9:1 ratio, so the lost volume causes rejection.

lessons.title: Tubes: colors, additives, tests and fill rules
lessons.body:
## Why the color means something

The cap color is shorthand for what is inside the tube, and what is inside determines what the lab can measure. Putting blood in the wrong tube does not give a slightly wrong answer; it usually gives no answer, and you get a phone call and a second stick.

| Cap | Additive | Common tests | Inversions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yellow bottles | SPS broth | Blood cultures | Per manufacturer |
| Light blue | Sodium citrate `3.2%` | PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer, fibrinogen | 3-4 |
| Red (plain glass) | None | Serum chemistry, serology, blood bank at some labs | 0-5 |
| Gold / red-grey SST | Clot activator + gel | CMP, BMP, troponin, lipase, TSH, most chemistries | 5 |
| Green | Lithium or sodium heparin | Stat chemistries, ammonia, many i-STAT cartridges | 8-10 |
| Lavender | K2 EDTA | CBC with differential, HbA1c, ESR | 8-10 |
| Pink | K2 EDTA | Type and screen, crossmatch | 8-10 |
| Gray | Sodium fluoride + potassium oxalate | Lactate (per lab), glucose, blood alcohol | 8-10 |
| Dark blue | Varies, trace-element free | Lead, zinc, copper, other trace metals | 8-10 |
| Yellow (ACD) | Acid citrate dextrose | HLA typing, paternity, some DNA studies | 8-10 |

## The fill rules that get specimens rejected

**Light blue must be filled exactly to the line.** The tube contains a fixed volume of citrate designed for a `9:1` ratio of blood to anticoagulant. Underfill it and the excess citrate binds extra calcium, falsely **prolonging** the PT and aPTT — which can look like a bleeding disorder that does not exist, or mask one that does. Most laboratories reject a citrate tube filled below about `90%`.

**Every additive tube needs the additive mixed in.** Invert gently, end over end, the number of times the manufacturer specifies — usually `8-10` for EDTA, heparin, fluoride and trace tubes, `3-4` for citrate, `5` for SST.

> **Trap:** Invert, never shake. Shaking shears red cells and hemolyzes the sample. Gentle, full, unhurried end-over-end turns — the tube should go completely upside down each time.

**Underfilled EDTA tubes** concentrate the anticoagulant, which shrinks red cells and falsely lowers hematocrit while raising the measured MCHC. **Overfilled** tubes clot, and a clotted CBC is unrunnable.

## Special handling

- **Ammonia** goes in a green or lavender tube depending on the lab, must go **on ice**, and must reach the lab fast — ammonia rises in a sitting sample.
- **Lactate** goes on ice in many laboratories, in a gray tube, though many emergency departments run it on a green-top by point-of-care analyzer within minutes instead. Follow your lab.
- **Blood alcohol for legal purposes** requires a **non-alcohol** skin prep, usually povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine, plus chain of custody. Cleaning with an isopropyl alcohol wipe gives the defense an argument.
- **Pink type and screen tubes** carry extra identification requirements at almost every hospital: a dedicated blood bank band with a unique number, the number written on the tube, and often a signature. Blood bank specimens are rejected for the smallest labeling defect, on purpose.

## Volumes and pediatrics

Adult tubes typically hold `2-10 mL`. Most chemistry panels need at least `1 mL` of serum, meaning roughly `2-3 mL` of whole blood, and a CBC needs about `1 mL`. A tube that comes back **QNS** (quantity not sufficient) means the lab could not run it.

Children and neonates use **microtainers** holding roughly `250-500 microliters`, filled from a heel stick in an infant or a fingerstick in an older child, with the same color coding and the same order of draw. Because volume matters so much in a small patient, decide the full list of tests before the stick.

> **On shift:** Before you walk into the room, look at the orders and lay out every tube you will need, in order. The two most common reasons for a second stick are a tube you did not bring and a tube you did not fill.
keyPoints: Light blue is citrate for coagulation and must be filled exactly to the line for a 9:1 ratio; underfill falsely prolongs PT and aPTT.
Gold SST covers most chemistries including troponin, lipase and TSH; lavender EDTA covers CBC and HbA1c; pink EDTA is type and screen.
Gray (fluoride/oxalate) is for glucose, lactate and alcohol; green heparin for stat chemistries and many i-STAT cartridges.
Invert 8-10 times for EDTA, heparin, fluoride and trace tubes, 3-4 for citrate, 5 for SST — invert, never shake.
Legal blood alcohol requires a non-alcohol skin prep and chain of custody; pediatric microtainers hold roughly 250-500 microliters.

checks.q: A light blue citrate tube is filled only two-thirds of the way. What happens?
choices: Nothing; the lab adjusts for volume
The excess citrate binds extra calcium and falsely prolongs the PT and aPTT, so the specimen is rejected
The tube clots
Potassium is falsely elevated
checks.why: The citrate volume is fixed for a 9:1 ratio with a full tube. Underfilling leaves excess anticoagulant, which prolongs clotting times and can mimic a bleeding disorder, so labs reject citrate tubes below about 90% fill.

checks.q: Which tube is used for a type and screen?
choices: Gold SST
Light blue
Pink EDTA, with additional blood bank identification requirements
Gray
checks.why: Pink EDTA tubes are the standard blood bank tube, and they carry extra identification requirements such as a dedicated band with a unique number recorded on the tube, because a labeling error here can cause a fatal transfusion reaction.

checks.q: How should an EDTA tube be mixed?
choices: Shaken vigorously 10 times
Inverted gently end over end 8 to 10 times
Left alone; the additive dissolves on its own
Inverted 3 times
checks.why: Gentle complete inversions distribute the anticoagulant without shearing red cells. Shaking hemolyzes the sample, and inadequate mixing lets the specimen clot, either of which makes the CBC unrunnable.

lessons.title: Venipuncture, step by step
lessons.body:
## Choosing the vein

The antecubital fossa — the crease at the front of the elbow — is the first place to look, because the veins there are large, close to the surface, and well anchored.

1. **Median cubital vein** — first choice. It sits in the middle, is well supported by tissue, moves least, and has the fewest nerves and arteries beneath it.
2. **Cephalic vein** — the thumb-side vein. Second choice. Often the only palpable vein in a larger arm, but it rolls more.
3. **Basilic vein** — the little-finger side. **Last choice in the antecubital fossa.** The brachial artery and the median nerve run directly beneath it. Nerve injury and arterial puncture happen here more than anywhere else.
4. **Dorsal hand veins** — usable with a smaller gauge and a shallow angle. More painful, more fragile, and more prone to hematoma.

Feel, do not just look. A good vein is **bouncy and springy** under the fingertip. A cord that is hard and rolls like a tendon is usually thrombosed. A structure that **pulses** is an artery — never puncture it deliberately.

## Where you never draw

- The arm on the side of a **mastectomy with lymph node dissection**, because of lymphedema risk — per current policy, ask the nurse rather than assuming, as guidance has softened for sentinel node procedures.
- An arm with a **dialysis fistula or graft**.
- **Above an infusing IV** on the same arm — the sample will be diluted with IV fluid. If it is unavoidable, draw **below** the IV after it has been stopped for at least `2 minutes`, note it, and prefer the other arm.
- Scarred, burned, tattooed-over-fresh, edematous, infected or hematoma-filled areas.
- The affected side of a stroke with paralysis, or a limb with a cast or recent surgery.

## The draw

1. Gather everything and lay the tubes out **in order of draw** before you start. Gloves on.
2. Position the arm supported and slightly downward, extended at the elbow.
3. Apply the tourniquet `3-4 inches` (about `7.5-10 cm`) above the intended site, tight enough to distend veins but never enough to obliterate the radial pulse.
4. Palpate and select. Have the patient make a fist — but **do not let them pump the fist**, which drives potassium out of muscle and falsely raises the result.
5. Clean with `70%` isopropyl alcohol in concentric circles or firm back-and-forth friction for about `30 seconds`, then **let it air dry completely**. Wet alcohol stings and hemolyzes the sample. Do not re-palpate a cleaned site with an ungloved finger.
6. **Release the tourniquet if more than 1 minute has passed** and re-apply just before puncture. A tourniquet left on longer causes hemoconcentration, falsely raising potassium, calcium, protein and hematocrit.
7. Anchor the vein by pulling the skin taut with your thumb `1-2 inches` below the site, thumb pulling downward and away. This is what stops the vein rolling, and it is the step most often skipped.
8. Insert **bevel up** at `15-30 degrees` to the skin, following the direction of the vein. A `21 G` needle is the adult standard; a `22-23 G` butterfly is for small, fragile or hand veins. Anything smaller than `23 G` risks hemolysis.
9. On flashback or the feel of give, lower the angle slightly, advance a few millimeters, hold steady, and engage the tubes in order. Change tubes on the holder without moving the needle.
10. **Release the tourniquet before the last tube finishes**, and always before withdrawing the needle, to lower venous pressure and reduce hematoma.
11. Withdraw the needle, activate the safety device immediately, and apply firm pressure with gauze for `3-5 minutes` — longer, up to `10 minutes` or more, for a patient on warfarin, a direct oral anticoagulant, clopidogrel or heparin. Keep the arm straight; bending the elbow over gauze causes bruising.
12. Invert each tube the required number of times, label at the bedside, and dispose of the needle in the sharps container — never recapped.

> **Key:** Tourniquet under one minute, alcohol fully dry, anchor the vein, and release the tourniquet before you pull the needle. Those four habits prevent most bad results and most hematomas.

> **Trap:** Two attempts, then get someone else. A third and fourth stick by the same person on the same patient does not usually work, and it costs the patient trust, tissue and time.
keyPoints: Median cubital first, cephalic second, basilic last — the brachial artery and median nerve lie under the basilic vein.
Never draw from a fistula or graft arm, above an infusing IV, or from scarred, burned, edematous or infected tissue.
Tourniquet 3-4 inches above the site and under 1 minute; longer causes hemoconcentration that falsely raises potassium.
Clean with alcohol for about 30 seconds and let it dry fully; anchor the vein; enter bevel up at 15-30 degrees with a 21 G needle or 22-23 G butterfly.
Release the tourniquet before withdrawing, hold pressure 3-5 minutes or longer on anticoagulants, and stop after two attempts.

checks.q: Why is the basilic vein the last choice in the antecubital fossa?
choices: It is too small to cannulate
The brachial artery and median nerve lie directly beneath it
It hemolyzes samples
It is only present in some patients
checks.why: Arterial puncture and nerve injury occur most often at the basilic vein because of what sits under it. The median cubital is better anchored and has no major artery or nerve beneath it.

checks.q: A tourniquet has been on for three minutes while you hunt for a vein. What should you do?
choices: Continue; time does not matter
Release it, wait about two minutes, and reapply just before puncture
Tighten it further
Draw quickly and note the time on the label
checks.why: A tourniquet over one minute causes hemoconcentration, falsely raising potassium, calcium, total protein and hematocrit. Releasing and reapplying restores normal conditions before the draw.

checks.q: Why should a patient not pump their fist during a draw?
choices: It collapses the vein
Muscle activity releases potassium and falsely elevates the result
It causes the tourniquet to slip
It increases pain
checks.why: Repeated muscle contraction drives potassium out of the muscle cells into local blood, producing a falsely high potassium. Making a fist once is fine; pumping it is not.

lessons.title: Hemolysis and rejected specimens
lessons.body:
## What hemolysis is and why it matters

Hemolysis is the rupture of red blood cells, spilling their contents into the plasma or serum. The sample turns pink or red instead of straw-colored, and the lab can see it instantly.

The inside of a red cell is a completely different chemical environment from the fluid around it. Red cells hold roughly `25` times more potassium inside than outside. Break some of them and you have added potassium to the specimen that was never free in the patient.

> **Key:** A hemolyzed potassium is falsely high, and that false result is indistinguishable from a real emergency without a redraw. It also falsely raises LDH, AST, magnesium and phosphate, and falsely lowers glucose and sodium.

Hemolysis is the number one reason specimens are rejected in emergency departments, with published rates commonly in the range of `5-10%` of ED draws — several times the rate from dedicated phlebotomy teams.

## The causes, and what each one teaches

**Drawing through an IV catheter or line.** The single biggest driver of ED hemolysis. Blood is pulled through a narrow plastic catheter, often against resistance, with turbulence at every junction. Draw from a fresh venipuncture whenever possible.

**A needle that is too small, or too large a syringe on a small needle.** Pulling hard on a `20 mL` syringe attached to a `23 G` butterfly generates enormous shear force. Match the syringe to the vein, and pull slowly.

**Forcing blood from a syringe through a needle into a tube.** Pushing blood through a small orifice under pressure shreds cells. Use a proper transfer device and let the tube's vacuum do the work.

**Shaking instead of inverting.** Gentle, complete, end-over-end inversions only.

**Tourniquet on too long,** or excessive fist pumping, or probing and redirecting the needle repeatedly.

**Underfilled tubes**, where the additive-to-blood ratio is wrong and the cells are chemically stressed.

**Wet alcohol.** Alcohol still on the skin enters with the needle and lyses cells directly. Let it dry.

**Extremes of temperature or rough transport** — a tube sent through a pneumatic tube system at high speed, left on a radiator, or left in a car.

## The other rejection reasons

**QNS — quantity not sufficient.** Not enough blood for the assay. Fill tubes to their stated volume, and when volume is tight, ask the lab which test to prioritize rather than splitting a tube.

**Clotted.** An EDTA or heparin tube that was not inverted promptly, or was filled too slowly, forms clots. A clotted CBC cannot be run, and a clotted specimen can damage the analyzer.

**Wrong tube, unlabeled, mislabeled, or expired tube.** Tubes have expiration dates; the vacuum degrades and the additive loses potency. Check the date on the rack at the start of your shift.

## The callback

When the lab calls with a critical potassium — say `6.8` — on a patient who is walking around, the conversation has three parts:

1. Was the specimen hemolyzed? The lab can usually tell you immediately, and often flags it on the result.
2. What was the order of draw, and was it drawn through an IV or after a lavender tube?
3. Redraw properly: a fresh venipuncture, a `21 G` needle, correct order, minimal tourniquet time, gentle inversions, and hand-walked or fast-tracked to the lab.

Meanwhile the patient still gets treated as though the number might be real until it is disproven — that is the provider's call, and it usually means an ECG looking for peaked T waves, widened QRS or a flattened P wave.

> **Trap:** Never assume a critical result is an artifact. Report it, redraw it, and let a clinician decide. The patient who is dismissed as probably hemolyzed and turns out to have a real potassium of `6.8` is a preventable arrest.

> **On shift:** Every hemolyzed tube costs a second stick, roughly an hour of turnaround, and a patient's trust. It is also the most preventable error in the whole job.
keyPoints: Hemolysis releases intracellular contents: potassium is falsely high, along with LDH, AST, magnesium and phosphate.
Drawing through an IV catheter is the largest single cause of hemolysis in an emergency department.
Other causes: needle too small, hard syringe pull, forcing blood into a tube, shaking, long tourniquet, underfilled tubes, wet alcohol.
Other rejection reasons are QNS, clotted, wrong tube, mislabeled and expired tubes.
A critical result is reported and redrawn, never dismissed as artifact by the person who drew it.

checks.q: Why does hemolysis falsely raise the potassium result?
choices: The additive contains potassium
Red cells hold far more potassium inside than the surrounding plasma, and rupture releases it into the sample
Hemolysis concentrates the plasma
It does not; hemolysis lowers potassium
checks.why: Intracellular potassium is roughly 25 times the plasma level, so even a small amount of cell rupture adds potassium that was never free in the patient. The same mechanism raises LDH, AST, magnesium and phosphate.

checks.q: What is the largest single cause of hemolyzed specimens in an emergency department?
choices: Cold storage
Drawing blood through an IV catheter or line
Using a 21 G needle
Labeling at the bedside
checks.why: Pulling blood through a narrow plastic catheter with turbulence at every junction shears red cells. A fresh venipuncture with a 21 G needle is the low-hemolysis standard.

checks.q: The lab calls with a potassium of 6.8 on a patient who feels well. What do you do?
choices: Tell them it must be hemolyzed and ignore it
Report it to the nurse, ask whether the sample was hemolyzed, and redraw properly from a fresh venipuncture
Repeat the draw from the same IV line
Wait for the next scheduled labs
checks.why: Only a clinician decides whether a critical value is real, and the patient is treated as if it might be until disproven. The redraw must avoid every hemolysis cause, which means a fresh stick rather than the same line.

lessons.title: Blood cultures done right
lessons.body:
## What you are actually testing

A blood culture asks whether bacteria are growing in the bloodstream. The bottle is a sterile broth; anything that gets into it will grow, including a skin bacterium your needle carried in.

That is the whole problem. A contaminated culture does not read as contaminated — it reads as a positive blood culture, and the patient may be admitted, given days of intravenous antibiotics, and have a central line placed for an organism that was never in their blood. Published estimates put the cost of a single contaminated blood culture in the thousands of dollars and several extra hospital days.

The accepted contamination rate target is **under `3%`**, and many laboratories track it by collector.

> **Key:** Skin prep and drying time are the entire difference between a useful culture and an expensive false alarm. There is no shortcut that works.

## Two sets, two sites

Standard adult practice is **two sets** of cultures, each set being an **aerobic** and an **anaerobic** bottle, drawn from **two separate venipuncture sites**.

The reason is interpretive. If one set grows a skin organism and the other is sterile, it is almost certainly contamination. If both sets grow the same organism, it is almost certainly real. A single set leaves the result uninterpretable.

Draw both sets before antibiotics whenever obtaining them will not meaningfully delay the drug. After the first dose, the yield falls sharply.

## Volume is the other half of sensitivity

Bacteria in blood are often present at very low concentrations, so **volume is the strongest single predictor of whether a culture grows**.

- Adults: `8-10 mL` per bottle, `20 mL` per set, `40 mL` total across two sets.
- Pediatric bottles are weight-based, commonly `1-3 mL` for infants and small children — check your department's chart. Overdrawing a small child is a real harm.

Underfilling an adult bottle by half can cut sensitivity substantially. Overfilling can cause false positives from the instrument's growth detection.

## The technique

1. Identify the patient, gather supplies, and check that the bottles are in date and the broth is clear.
2. **Prepare the bottle tops.** Pop the caps, scrub each rubber septum with `70%` alcohol, and let them dry. The septum is not sterile under the cap.
3. **Apply the tourniquet and find the vein first, before the skin prep** — so you are not re-palpating sterile skin later.
4. **Scrub the skin with chlorhexidine-alcohol** for a full `30 seconds` using firm back-and-forth friction, then let it dry completely, at least `30 seconds` and per the manufacturer. Povidone-iodine is an alternative and needs about `2 minutes` of drying. Chlorhexidine is not used on infants under 2 months in many protocols; use povidone-iodine there per policy.
5. **Do not touch the site again.** If you must re-palpate, do it above the prepped area, or re-prep with a sterile glove.
6. Draw.
7. **Inoculate the bottles.** Fill to the marked line, and check the volume against the graduations, not by feel.
8. Label at the bedside with site and time, and get them to the lab promptly. Do not refrigerate.

## Aerobic or anaerobic first, and why the answer flips

This is the classic exam question, and the logic is about **air**.

- **With a butterfly set,** the tubing contains roughly `0.5 mL` of air that will be pushed into the first bottle. Air belongs in the aerobic bottle, so **aerobic first**.
- **With a syringe,** there is no air in the line, and the anaerobic organisms are the more fragile, harder-to-recover ones. So **anaerobic first**, to protect them from the air that will enter as the syringe empties.

> **Trap:** If only one bottle's worth of blood can be obtained, most laboratories want the **aerobic** bottle filled, because most bloodstream pathogens are aerobes or facultative. Confirm your lab's rule.

> **On shift:** Cultures drawn from a central line have a higher contamination rate and are generally reserved for suspected line infection, where a paired peripheral and line set is drawn deliberately. Peripheral venipuncture is the default.
keyPoints: Two sets from two separate sites, each set an aerobic plus an anaerobic bottle, drawn before antibiotics when possible.
Adults: 8-10 mL per bottle, 20 mL per set, 40 mL total; pediatric volumes are weight-based and much smaller.
Scrub the skin with chlorhexidine-alcohol for 30 seconds and let it dry fully; scrub the bottle septa with alcohol too.
Butterfly: aerobic bottle first, because tubing air belongs there. Syringe: anaerobic first, to protect fragile anaerobes.
Contamination rate target is under 3%, and a contaminated culture costs days of unnecessary antibiotics.

checks.q: You are drawing blood cultures with a butterfly set. Which bottle do you fill first?
choices: Anaerobic, because anaerobes are fragile
Aerobic, because the tubing air will be pushed into the first bottle
Either; it makes no difference
Whichever has the larger volume marked
checks.why: Butterfly tubing holds about 0.5 mL of air. Air harms anaerobic recovery, so it goes into the aerobic bottle. With a syringe there is no line air, so the anaerobic bottle goes first to protect the fragile anaerobes.

checks.q: Why are two sets drawn from two separate sites?
choices: To double the total volume only
So that one set can be repeated if it spills
Because growth in one set only suggests contamination, while growth in both suggests real bacteremia
Because each site tests a different organism
checks.why: Two sets make the result interpretable. A single set that grows a skin organism cannot be distinguished from contamination, and a contaminated culture leads to days of unnecessary antibiotics and sometimes a central line.

checks.q: What adult volume goes into each blood culture bottle?
choices: 1-3 mL
4-5 mL
20 mL
checks.why: Volume is the strongest predictor of whether a culture grows, and the adult standard is 8 to 10 mL per bottle, 20 mL per set. 1-3 mL is a pediatric volume, and 20 mL in one bottle is an overfill.

lessons.title: Difficult draws, and when to stop
lessons.body:
## Why a vein hides

Veins are hard to find for a small number of reasons, and each one has a different fix: the patient is cold (veins constrict), dry (low volume means flat veins), in shock (peripheral vasoconstriction), obese (veins are deep but present), elderly (veins are fragile and roll in loose tissue), a long-term intravenous drug user or a frequent-draw patient (veins are scarred and thrombosed), or an oncology patient with years of chemotherapy.

## Techniques that actually work

**Warmth.** A warm pack or a warm moist towel over the site for `3-5 minutes` dilates veins measurably. This is the highest-yield trick in the whole list and the most under-used.

**Gravity.** Let the arm hang below the level of the heart for a minute or two before applying the tourniquet.

**Hydration and position.** A dehydrated patient with fluids running will be easier in twenty minutes than right now. If the draw is not time-critical, say so.

**Light tapping or stroking**, upward along the vein. Firm slapping causes hemolysis and bruising — stroke, do not slap.

**Blood pressure cuff** inflated to about `40 mmHg`, below diastolic, is a more even and adjustable tourniquet than a rubber band.

**Change the target.** Dorsal hand veins with a `23 G` butterfly and a shallow `10-15 degree` angle. The forearm, where the cephalic runs a long straight course. The thumb-side wrist vein, which is painful and used sparingly.

**Turn off the room lights** and use a vein finder or transillumination device if your department has one.

## When to hand it off

**Two attempts, then get someone else.** This is standard practice in nearly every hospital's phlebotomy policy and it exists because success rates fall with each attempt by the same person, while pain, hematoma and patient distress climb.

Hand off to a more experienced technician or nurse. The next escalation is **ultrasound-guided access**, performed by a trained nurse or provider, which is the standard answer for the known difficult-access patient rather than a last resort after six failed sticks.

For a critically ill patient in whom no access can be obtained, **intraosseous (IO) access** — a drill-placed needle into the bone marrow of the proximal tibia, proximal humerus or distal femur — provides immediate access for fluids, drugs and most labs. It is placed by a credentialed nurse or provider. Your job is to know where the drill and the correct needle sizes are, and to recognize when the room has reached that point.

> **Key:** Stopping after two attempts is not failure. It is the standard, and it protects the patient from the predictable outcome of a third attempt by the same hands.

## What to say to the patient

Difficult-access patients have usually been stuck many times and often know their own veins better than you do. Ask them: where do people usually get you, which arm works, is there a spot that never works. That question is faster than any device.

Tell them what you are doing, tell them when the stick is coming, and do not promise it will not hurt. If you miss, say so plainly, apologize once, and hand off without drama.

> **On shift:** Ask the patient first, warm the arm second, and bring help third. That order solves most of these.
keyPoints: Cold, dehydration, shock, obesity, age and scarring each make veins hard for a different reason with a different fix.
Warmth for 3-5 minutes, gravity, gentle stroking, and a BP cuff at about 40 mmHg are the highest-yield techniques.
Two attempts, then hand off — success rates fall and harm rises with each further attempt by the same person.
Ultrasound-guided access by a trained nurse or provider is the standard next step, not a last resort.
Intraosseous access is for the critically ill patient with no obtainable access, placed by a credentialed clinician.

checks.q: What is the highest-yield and most under-used technique for a difficult vein?
choices: Slapping the site firmly
Applying warmth to the site for 3 to 5 minutes
Using a larger needle
Tightening the tourniquet further
checks.why: Warmth causes measurable vasodilation. Slapping hemolyzes and bruises, a larger needle does not help a vein you cannot find, and an over-tight tourniquet collapses veins and causes hemoconcentration.

checks.q: How many attempts should one person make before handing off?
choices: One
Two
Four
As many as needed until successful
checks.why: Two attempts is the standard policy in nearly every hospital. Success rates fall with each further attempt by the same person, while pain, hematoma and distress rise, so handing off is the correct action, not a failure.

checks.q: A critically ill patient in shock has no obtainable peripheral access. What is the appropriate escalation?
choices: Repeated attempts at hand veins
Intraosseous access placed by a credentialed clinician
Waiting for the patient to be rehydrated
Drawing from an artery
checks.why: IO access into the proximal tibia, humerus or distal femur gives immediate access for fluids, drugs and most labs in a patient who cannot wait. Repeated peripheral attempts waste the time that matters, and arterial draws are not for routine access.

lessons.title: IV catheter insertion and complications
lessons.body:
## Gauge, color, and what each one is for

In many New Jersey emergency departments, technicians are credentialed to start peripheral IVs after department training. Scope varies by hospital, so confirm yours.

Catheter gauge runs backwards: the **smaller the number, the larger the bore**.

| Gauge | Color | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 14 | Orange | Massive transfusion, major trauma resuscitation |
| 16 | Gray | Trauma, major GI bleed, rapid volume |
| 18 | Green | Blood products, CT contrast, surgery |
| 20 | Pink | The general adult workhorse; acceptable for most CT contrast |
| 22 | Blue | Fragile veins, elderly, most pediatric patients |
| 24 | Yellow | Neonates, infants, very fragile veins |

For **CT with contrast**, an **`18-20 G` in the antecubital fossa** is the usual requirement, because power injectors push contrast at high flow rates and a smaller or more distal catheter can rupture the vein. Confirm against the radiology protocol.

For **trauma, major bleeding or shock**, two large-bore lines (`14-16 G`) in the antecubital fossae are the goal. Flow rises steeply with catheter radius and falls with length, so a short fat line beats a long thin one.

Prefer the **forearm** for routine access: the catheter sits in a straight section, the patient can bend the elbow, and it lasts longer. The antecubital is fast and large-bore but kinks with flexion and occludes pumps.

## The insertion

1. Gather everything, including flush, dressing and securement, before you start.
2. Tourniquet `3-4 inches` above, select the vein, clean with chlorhexidine for `30 seconds` and let it dry.
3. Anchor the skin taut below the site.
4. Enter **bevel up at `10-30 degrees`**, shallower than a venipuncture because you are threading a catheter.
5. **First flashback** means the needle tip is in the vein — but the catheter tip may not be.
6. **Lower the angle nearly flat and advance the whole unit another `1-2 mm`** so the plastic catheter is inside the lumen. This step is where most failures happen.
7. **Advance the catheter off the needle**, holding the needle still. Never re-advance the needle into a partly withdrawn catheter; it can shear the plastic and embolize it.
8. Release the tourniquet, press over the catheter tip, withdraw the needle, and **activate the safety mechanism immediately**.
9. Attach the extension set, **flush with `5-10 mL` of normal saline** while watching and feeling the site.
10. Secure with a transparent dressing so the site stays visible, and label with date, time, gauge and initials.

**Drawing labs off a fresh IV start** is acceptable in most departments at the moment of insertion, before any fluid runs. It hemolyzes more often than a clean venipuncture, so use the largest reasonable gauge and draw gently — and never draw from a line already infusing.

## Complications and what each one looks like

| Problem | What you see | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Infiltration** | Swelling, coolness, pallor, tightness, sluggish flow, no blood return. Non-vesicant fluid in the tissue | Stop infusion, remove catheter, elevate, warm or cool per protocol, notify nurse |
| **Extravasation** | Same picture but with a vesicant drug — contrast, vasopressors, chemotherapy, calcium | **Stop immediately, do not remove the catheter yet**, aspirate if instructed, notify nurse and provider at once. Can cause tissue necrosis |
| **Phlebitis** | Redness, warmth, pain, a palpable cord along the vein. Inflammation, not leakage | Stop infusion, remove catheter, warm compress, notify nurse |
| **Hematoma** | Immediate swelling and bruising at the stick | Remove, hold firm pressure, elevate |
| **Arterial puncture** | Bright red blood, pulsatile, fills the chamber under its own pressure | **Remove immediately and hold firm pressure for at least `5-10 minutes`**, then notify the nurse and provider and document |

> **Key:** Infiltration and extravasation look identical. The difference is what was infusing — and with a vesicant, the catheter stays in until a clinician decides, because it may be the route for aspiration or an antidote.

> **Trap:** Never draw blood from a line that is currently infusing fluid. The sample is diluted, and a diluted potassium or glucose gets acted on before anyone realizes.
keyPoints: Smaller gauge number means larger bore: 14 orange, 16 gray, 18 green, 20 pink, 22 blue, 24 yellow.
CT contrast usually needs an 18-20 G in the antecubital fossa; trauma wants two large-bore 14-16 G lines.
Advance the unit 1-2 mm after flashback so the catheter is in the lumen, then advance the catheter off the needle — never re-advance the needle.
Flush with 5-10 mL saline, secure with a transparent dressing, and label with date, time, gauge and initials.
Infiltration and extravasation look the same; with a vesicant the catheter stays in until a clinician decides. Arterial puncture means remove and hold pressure 5-10 minutes.

checks.q: A CT with contrast is ordered. Which access is usually required?
choices: A 22 G in the hand
An 18 to 20 G in the antecubital fossa
A 24 G anywhere
Any gauge, as long as it flushes
checks.why: Power injectors push contrast at high flow rates, so a small or distal catheter can rupture the vein. An 18-20 G in the antecubital fossa is the common requirement, confirmed against the radiology protocol.

checks.q: You get flashback in the chamber. What is the next step?
choices: Advance the catheter off the needle immediately
Lower the angle and advance the whole unit 1-2 mm, then advance the catheter off the needle
Withdraw the needle and flush
Release the tourniquet and tape it down
checks.why: Flashback means the needle tip is in the vein, but the catheter tip sits slightly behind it and may still be in the wall. Advancing the catheter without that extra 1-2 mm is the most common cause of a failed start.

checks.q: IV contrast has infiltrated into the tissue of the forearm. What do you do?
choices: Remove the catheter and apply a warm compress
Flush the line to clear it
Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in place, and notify the nurse and provider immediately
Restart the infusion at a slower rate
checks.why: Contrast is a vesicant, so this is extravasation, which can cause tissue necrosis. The catheter stays in because it may be needed for aspiration or an antidote, and a clinician makes that decision, not the person who found it.

lessons.title: Point-of-care testing and specimen handling
lessons.body:
## Point-of-care testing

**Fingerstick glucose.** Warm the hand, clean with alcohol and let it dry, lance the **side** of the fingertip (fewer nerve endings, better blood flow than the pad), **wipe away the first drop** because it contains tissue fluid and any residual sugar on the skin, then apply the second drop to the strip without squeezing hard. Milking the finger dilutes the sample with tissue fluid and falsely lowers the reading.

A fingerstick is **unreliable in shock, severe dehydration, hypothermia, peripheral edema and severe anemia**, because it measures capillary blood from tissue that is not being perfused. In any of those, or whenever the reading does not match the patient, send a venous or point-of-care blood gas glucose.

**i-STAT and similar analyzers** run cartridges from a small whole-blood sample. Cartridges are temperature- and time-sensitive: fill without air bubbles, cap, and insert within the manufacturer's window. Common cartridges cover chemistry and electrolytes, troponin, lactate and blood gases, and an air bubble is the usual cause of an error code.

**Urine dipstick** is read at the times printed on the bottle — different pads read at different intervals, and a strip read late gives falsely positive glucose, ketones and leukocytes. **Urine hCG** needs a clean specimen and the full read time; a faint line inside the window is positive, a line appearing after it is not.

**Rapid respiratory swabs** (strep, influenza, COVID, RSV) live or die on technique. A nasopharyngeal swab goes **straight back along the floor of the nose, parallel to the palate — not upward** — to roughly the nostril-to-ear distance, then rotates in place for several seconds. A shallow swab produces a false negative. A throat swab touches both tonsils and the posterior pharynx, avoiding the tongue and cheeks.

**Breath alcohol** devices need a waiting period, commonly `15-20 minutes` with nothing in the mouth, so mouth alcohol does not contaminate the reading.

Every point-of-care device requires documented **quality control** at your policy's interval, with the operator identified. A device that has not passed QC does not produce a usable result.

## Specimen collection instructions

**Clean-catch urine, women:** separate the labia and keep them separated, wipe front to back with each wipe, begin voiding into the toilet, move the cup into the stream for the middle portion, finish in the toilet. **Men:** retract the foreskin if uncircumcised, clean the tip, void the first portion into the toilet, catch the midstream.

A **straight catheterization** specimen is used when a clean catch is impossible or repeatedly contaminated. A specimen from an indwelling Foley comes from the **cleaned sampling port**, never the drainage bag — bag urine has been growing organisms for hours.

**Stool** goes in a clean dry container with no urine or toilet water. **Sputum** is a deep cough specimen, not saliva. **Wound cultures** sample deep tissue or the advancing edge after the surface is cleaned, not the crust or drainage.

## Chain of custody

Legal blood alcohol and forensic drug screens require an unbroken documented chain: a **non-alcohol skin prep**, a tamper-evident seal applied in the patient's presence, every transfer signed and timed, and the specimen never left unattended. A missed step can make the result inadmissible, so ask before the needle goes in.

## Transport and the tube system

- **On ice:** ammonia, lactate (per lab policy), delayed blood gases.
- **Protected from light:** bilirubin.
- **Kept at `37 C`:** cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins.
- **Room temperature and prompt:** most everything else. Potassium rises in a specimen that sits, and glucose falls unless it is in a fluoride tube.

Several specimens do not go by **pneumatic tube**: blood bank specimens at many hospitals, blood gases, cryoprecipitate, cold agglutinins, large-volume containers, and anything glass or leakable. Tubes accelerate hard enough to hemolyze samples. Hand-walk anything on ice, anything time-critical, and anything your policy names.

## Needlestick protocol

If you sustain a needlestick or a splash: wash the site immediately with soap and water (flush mucous membranes or eyes with water or saline for `15 minutes`), do not squeeze the wound or apply bleach, report to your supervisor immediately, go to employee health or the emergency department per policy, and get source-patient testing and baseline labs started. Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV is most effective when started within hours — ideally under `2 hours` and generally within `72 hours` — so the report is time-critical, not paperwork you file at the end of the shift.

> **Key:** Report every exposure the moment it happens. The clock on prophylaxis starts at the stick, not at the end of your shift.
keyPoints: Fingerstick: lance the side of the fingertip, wipe away the first drop, do not milk. Unreliable in shock, edema, hypothermia and severe anemia.
i-STAT cartridges are time- and temperature-sensitive; air bubbles are the usual cause of an error, and QC must be current and documented.
Nasopharyngeal swabs go straight back along the nasal floor, not upward, to about nostril-to-ear depth and rotate in place.
Foley samples come from the cleaned sampling port, never the drainage bag; legal alcohol needs non-alcohol prep and chain of custody.
Ammonia and lactate go on ice; blood bank specimens, blood gases and glass tubes generally do not go in the pneumatic tube.

checks.q: Why is the first drop of blood wiped away in a fingerstick glucose?
choices: It is too small to read
It contains tissue fluid and any residual sugar on the skin, which distorts the result
It clots faster than later drops
It is required for infection control only
checks.why: The first drop is diluted by interstitial fluid and can carry surface contamination such as a sugary residue on the fingers. The second drop reflects capillary blood, provided the finger is not milked.

checks.q: A urine specimen is needed on a patient with an indwelling Foley catheter. Where does it come from?
choices: The drainage bag
The cleaned sampling port on the tubing
A fresh straight catheterization in addition to the Foley
Any point after disconnecting the tubing
checks.why: Bag urine has been sitting for hours and has grown organisms, making it uninterpretable. The sampling port is cleaned and aspirated. Disconnecting the closed system introduces infection risk and is avoided.

checks.q: You sustain a needlestick from a used device. What is the first priority?
choices: Finish the current patient and report at the end of shift
Squeeze the wound to express blood, then apply bleach
Wash immediately with soap and water and report at once, because HIV prophylaxis is most effective within hours
File an incident report only if the source patient is known to be positive
checks.why: Post-exposure prophylaxis works best when started within hours and generally within 72 hours, so immediate reporting is clinical care, not paperwork. Squeezing and bleach cause tissue damage without reducing transmission risk.

cards.front: What two identifiers are used before a blood draw, and which are never acceptable?
cards.back: Usually full name and date of birth, matched to the wristband and the label. Room number and bed location are never acceptable identifiers.

cards.front: What is the difference between active and passive patient identification?
cards.back: Active: tell me your full name and date of birth. Passive: are you Mr. Klein? A confused, sedated or polite patient agrees to any name offered, so only active identification is acceptable.

cards.front: When and where are specimen tubes labeled?
cards.back: At the bedside, immediately after the draw, before leaving the room, with the patient still present. Never pre-labeled and never labeled at a counter.

cards.front: What five elements belong on a specimen label?
cards.back: Patient's full name, a second identifier such as date of birth or medical record number, the date, the exact collection time, and your initials or identification.

cards.front: Why is the exact collection time on the label clinically important?
cards.back: Troponin timing, drug levels, lactate clearance and blood alcohol are all interpreted against collection time. A receipt-time stamp distorts whether a value is rising or falling.

cards.front: State the order of draw.
cards.back: Blood culture bottles, light blue citrate, red or gold serum, green heparin, lavender or pink EDTA, gray fluoride/oxalate. Boys Love Ravishing Girls Like Grandma.

cards.front: What happens if a lavender tube is drawn before a chemistry tube?
cards.back: EDTA carryover falsely raises potassium, because the anticoagulant is a potassium salt, and falsely lowers calcium, because EDTA binds calcium. It is the classic cause of a critical potassium in a well patient.

cards.front: What happens if a light blue tube is drawn after a heparin or serum tube?
cards.back: Heparin or clot activator carryover falsely shortens the PT and aPTT. Because coagulation results drive anticoagulant dosing, the consequence is a real dose error.

cards.front: Why is a discard tube drawn first when using a butterfly with a light blue tube?
cards.back: The butterfly tubing holds roughly `0.5 mL` of air that consumes part of the first tube's vacuum. A citrate tube must fill exactly to the line for the `9:1` ratio, so the lost volume causes rejection.

cards.front: What is in a light blue tube, what tests does it run, and what is its fill rule?
cards.back: Sodium citrate `3.2%`. PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer, fibrinogen. It must be filled exactly to the line for a `9:1` blood-to-citrate ratio, inverted 3-4 times.

cards.front: What does a gold or red-grey SST tube contain and what runs on it?
cards.back: Clot activator plus separator gel. CMP, BMP, troponin, lipase, TSH and most chemistries. Invert 5 times.

cards.front: What does a lavender tube contain and what runs on it?
cards.back: K2 EDTA. CBC with differential, HbA1c, ESR. Invert 8-10 times. Ammonia may go in lavender or green depending on the lab and must go on ice.

cards.front: What is the pink tube for, and what is special about it?
cards.back: K2 EDTA for type and screen and crossmatch. It carries extra identification requirements — usually a dedicated blood bank band with a unique number recorded on the tube — and is rejected for the smallest labeling defect.

cards.front: What does a gray tube contain and what runs on it?
cards.back: Sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate. Glucose, lactate (per lab) and blood alcohol. The fluoride stops glycolysis so glucose does not fall in the tube. Invert 8-10 times.

cards.front: What does a green tube contain and what is it used for?
cards.back: Lithium or sodium heparin. Stat chemistries, ammonia, and many i-STAT cartridges. Invert 8-10 times.

cards.front: How many inversions do the common tubes need?
cards.back: EDTA, heparin, fluoride and trace tubes 8-10; citrate 3-4; SST 5. Gentle end-over-end inversions, never shaking.

cards.front: What is a microtainer and how much does it hold?
cards.back: A pediatric collection tube holding roughly `250-500 microliters`, filled from a heel stick in an infant or a fingerstick in an older child, using the same color coding and order of draw.

cards.front: Rank the antecubital veins in order of preference and say why.
cards.back: Median cubital first — well anchored, no major artery or nerve beneath. Cephalic second, though it rolls. Basilic last, because the brachial artery and median nerve lie directly under it.

cards.front: How does a good vein feel, and how do you know a structure is an artery?
cards.back: A good vein is bouncy and springy under the fingertip. A hard rolling cord is usually thrombosed. Anything that pulses is an artery and is never punctured deliberately.

cards.front: List the sites you never draw from.
cards.back: A fistula or graft arm, a mastectomy side with node dissection (ask the nurse), above an infusing IV, and scarred, burned, edematous, infected or hematoma-filled tissue. Avoid a paralyzed or casted limb.

cards.front: Where does the tourniquet go, and how long may it stay on?
cards.back: `3-4 inches` above the site, tight enough to distend veins but never enough to obliterate the radial pulse, for under `1 minute`. Longer causes hemoconcentration that falsely raises potassium, calcium, protein and hematocrit.

cards.front: How long do you clean a venipuncture site with alcohol, and what must happen next?
cards.back: About `30 seconds` of firm friction with `70%` isopropyl alcohol, then let it air dry completely. Wet alcohol stings and hemolyzes the sample.

cards.front: Why should a patient not pump their fist during a draw?
cards.back: Repeated muscle contraction drives potassium out of muscle cells into the local blood, falsely raising the potassium result. Making a fist once is fine.

cards.front: What needle gauge and angle are standard for adult venipuncture?
cards.back: `21 G` straight needle for most adults, `22-23 G` butterfly for small, fragile or hand veins. Bevel up at `15-30 degrees`. Anything smaller than `23 G` risks hemolysis.

cards.front: How do you anchor a vein, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Pull the skin taut with your thumb `1-2 inches` below the site, pulling downward and away. It is what stops the vein rolling, and it is the step most often skipped.

cards.front: When is the tourniquet released, and how long do you hold pressure afterward?
cards.back: Released before the last tube finishes and always before the needle is withdrawn. Hold firm gauze pressure `3-5 minutes`, or `10 minutes` or more on anticoagulants, with the arm straight.

cards.front: How many venipuncture attempts before handing off?
cards.back: Two. A third and fourth attempt by the same person rarely succeeds and costs the patient tissue, trust and time. Hand off to a more experienced colleague.

cards.front: What is hemolysis, and which results does it distort?
cards.back: Rupture of red cells spilling contents into the serum. Falsely raises potassium, LDH, AST, magnesium and phosphate; falsely lowers glucose and sodium. The sample looks pink or red.

cards.front: Why does hemolysis raise potassium so dramatically?
cards.back: Red cells hold roughly `25` times more potassium inside than the plasma around them, so even minor rupture adds potassium that was never free in the patient.

cards.front: What is the biggest single cause of hemolyzed specimens in an emergency department?
cards.back: Drawing blood through an IV catheter or line. Blood is pulled through a narrow plastic catheter with turbulence at every junction, shearing red cells.

cards.front: Name six causes of hemolysis besides drawing through a line.
cards.back: A needle too small, a hard pull on a large syringe, forcing blood through a needle into a tube, shaking instead of inverting, a tourniquet left on too long, and underfilled tubes. Wet alcohol also lyses cells.

cards.front: Besides hemolysis, what are the common reasons a lab rejects a specimen?
cards.back: QNS (quantity not sufficient), clotted, wrong tube, unlabeled or mislabeled, and an expired tube whose vacuum and additive have degraded.

cards.front: How do you redraw after a suspected hemolyzed potassium?
cards.back: Fresh venipuncture, not the IV line. `21 G` needle, correct order of draw, tourniquet under a minute, alcohol fully dry, gentle inversions, and hand-walk it to the lab.

cards.front: Can you dismiss a critical potassium as hemolysis yourself?
cards.back: No. Report it, redraw properly, and let the clinician decide. The patient is treated as if it might be real until disproven — usually with an ECG looking for peaked T waves or a widened QRS.

cards.front: How many blood culture sets and sites, and what does each set contain?
cards.back: Two sets from two separate venipuncture sites, each set an aerobic plus an anaerobic bottle. Growth in one set only suggests contamination; growth in both suggests real bacteremia.

cards.front: What volume goes in each adult blood culture bottle?
cards.back: `8-10 mL` per bottle, `20 mL` per set, `40 mL` across two sets. Volume is the strongest single predictor of whether a culture grows.

cards.front: How do you prep the skin for a blood culture?
cards.back: Scrub with chlorhexidine-alcohol for a full `30 seconds` with firm friction, then let it dry completely. Povidone-iodine is the alternative and needs about `2 minutes` to dry. Do not re-touch the site.

cards.front: Do you clean the blood culture bottle tops, and why?
cards.back: Yes — scrub each rubber septum with `70%` alcohol and let it dry. The septum is not sterile under the cap, and anything on it goes straight into a sterile broth.

cards.front: Which culture bottle is filled first with a butterfly, and which with a syringe?
cards.back: Butterfly: aerobic first, because the tubing's `0.5 mL` of air belongs there. Syringe: anaerobic first, because there is no line air and anaerobes are the more fragile organisms.

cards.front: What is the target blood culture contamination rate, and what does one contaminant cost?
cards.back: Under `3%`. A single contaminated culture typically means days of unnecessary intravenous antibiotics, extra hospital days, sometimes a central line, and thousands of dollars.

cards.front: When must blood cultures be drawn relative to antibiotics?
cards.back: Before the first dose, whenever obtaining them will not meaningfully delay the drug. Yield falls sharply once antibiotics are in, and the organism may never be identified.

cards.front: What is the highest-yield technique for a hard-to-find vein?
cards.back: Warmth — a warm pack or warm moist towel over the site for `3-5 minutes` produces measurable vasodilation. It is the most under-used trick in phlebotomy.

cards.front: What is the escalation path after two failed attempts?
cards.back: Hand off to a more experienced technician or nurse, then ultrasound-guided access by a trained nurse or provider. For a critically ill patient with no access, intraosseous placement by a credentialed clinician.

cards.front: Where is intraosseous access placed, and what is it used for?
cards.back: A drill-placed needle into the proximal tibia, proximal humerus or distal femur. It gives immediate access for fluids, drugs and most labs in a critically ill patient with no obtainable IV.

cards.front: Match IV catheter gauges to their colors.
cards.back: 14 orange, 16 gray, 18 green, 20 pink, 22 blue, 24 yellow. The smaller the number, the larger the bore.

cards.front: What IV access does a CT with contrast usually require?
cards.back: An `18-20 G` in the antecubital fossa. Power injectors push contrast at high flow rates, and a smaller or more distal catheter can rupture the vein. Confirm against the radiology protocol.

cards.front: What access does a trauma or major GI bleed need, and why?
cards.back: Two large-bore lines, `14-16 G`, in the antecubital fossae. Flow rises steeply with catheter radius and falls with length, so short and fat beats long and thin for resuscitation.

cards.front: What do you do immediately after flashback on an IV start?
cards.back: Lower the angle nearly flat and advance the whole unit another `1-2 mm` so the catheter tip is inside the lumen, then hold the needle still and advance the catheter off it.

cards.front: Why must you never re-advance the needle into a partly withdrawn catheter?
cards.back: The needle tip can shear the plastic catheter, sending a fragment into the circulation as a catheter embolus. If the attempt fails, remove the whole unit and start over.

cards.front: How do you finish an IV start?
cards.back: Flush with `5-10 mL` of normal saline while watching and feeling the site, secure with a transparent dressing so the site stays visible, and label with date, time, gauge and your initials.

cards.front: When is it acceptable to draw labs from an IV catheter?
cards.back: At the moment of a fresh start, before any fluid runs. It carries a higher hemolysis rate, so use the largest reasonable gauge and draw gently. Never draw from a line that is currently infusing.

cards.front: How do infiltration and extravasation differ, and how does the response differ?
cards.back: Both show swelling, coolness, pallor and no blood return. Extravasation involves a vesicant such as contrast, a vasopressor or chemotherapy. With a vesicant, stop but leave the catheter in and notify the provider immediately.

cards.front: How does phlebitis present, and what do you do?
cards.back: Redness, warmth, pain and a palpable cord along the vein — inflammation, not leakage. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm compress, notify the nurse.

cards.front: How do you recognize and handle an accidental arterial puncture?
cards.back: Bright red blood that pulses and fills the chamber under its own pressure. Remove immediately, hold firm pressure for at least `5-10 minutes`, then notify the nurse and provider and document.

cards.front: Describe correct fingerstick glucose technique.
cards.back: Warm the hand, clean with alcohol and let it dry, lance the side of the fingertip, wipe away the first drop, apply the second drop without milking the finger.

cards.front: When is a fingerstick glucose unreliable?
cards.back: Shock, severe dehydration, hypothermia, peripheral edema and severe anemia — any state where the fingertip is not well perfused. Send a venous or blood gas glucose instead.

cards.front: What is the usual cause of an i-STAT cartridge error?
cards.back: An air bubble in the sample well. Cartridges are also temperature- and time-sensitive and must be filled, capped and inserted within the manufacturer's window.

cards.front: How is a nasopharyngeal swab performed correctly?
cards.back: Straight back along the floor of the nose, parallel to the palate — never angled upward — to roughly the nostril-to-ear distance, then rotated in place for several seconds. A shallow swab gives a false negative.

cards.front: How do you instruct a woman for a clean-catch urine?
cards.back: Separate the labia and keep them separated, wipe front to back with each wipe, begin urinating into the toilet, move the cup into the stream for the middle portion, finish in the toilet.

cards.front: Where does a urine specimen come from on a catheterized patient?
cards.back: The cleaned sampling port on the tubing, aspirated with a syringe. Never from the drainage bag, where urine has been sitting and growing organisms for hours.

cards.front: What does chain of custody require?
cards.back: A non-alcohol skin prep, a tamper-evident seal applied in the patient's presence, every transfer signed and timed, and the specimen never left unattended. A missed step can make the result inadmissible.

cards.front: Which specimens go on ice, and which need other special handling?
cards.back: On ice: ammonia, lactate per lab policy, and delayed blood gases. Protected from light: bilirubin. Kept at `37 C`: cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins.

cards.front: What generally cannot go in the pneumatic tube system?
cards.back: Blood bank specimens at many hospitals, blood gases, cryoprecipitate, cold agglutinins, large-volume containers, glass tubes, and anything that could leak. Tube acceleration hemolyzes samples.

cards.front: What is the needlestick protocol?
cards.back: Wash with soap and water immediately (flush eyes or mucous membranes `15 minutes`), do not squeeze or use bleach, report at once, and get source testing and baseline labs. HIV prophylaxis works best within hours, generally within `72 hours`.

quiz.q: You are about to draw blood on an elderly patient who is slightly confused. What is the correct identification method?
choices: Ask are you Mrs. Alvarez and proceed if she nods
Confirm the room number matches the requisition
Ask her to state her full name and date of birth, then match it to the wristband and the labels
Ask the family member at the bedside only
quiz.why: Two identifiers, asked actively, matched to band and label. A confused patient will agree to any name offered, room number is never an acceptable identifier, and family confirmation supplements but does not replace the wristband.

quiz.q: When should specimen tubes be labeled?
choices: At the bedside immediately after the draw, with the patient present
Before the draw so nothing is forgotten
At the counter outside the room
When the specimens arrive in the lab
quiz.why: Labeling at the bedside is the only point at which the patient, the band and the tube are all together. Pre-labeling produces a labeled tube with the wrong blood if the stick fails, and counter labeling is the classic path to a fatal swap.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly represents the order of draw?
choices: Light blue, blood cultures, gold, lavender, green, gray
Blood cultures, light blue, gold, green, lavender, gray
Gold, light blue, blood cultures, green, gray, lavender
Blood cultures, lavender, light blue, green, gold, gray
quiz.why: Cultures first to protect sterility, then citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA and fluoride last. Any sequence placing lavender before a chemistry tube risks EDTA carryover, and any sequence placing cultures after another tube risks contaminating a sterile bottle.

quiz.q: A basic metabolic panel returns a potassium of 7.1 and a calcium of 6.2 on an asymptomatic patient. The tubes were drawn lavender first, then gold. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: True hyperkalemia from renal failure
Tourniquet released too early
An underfilled citrate tube
EDTA carryover from the lavender tube, which raises potassium and binds calcium
quiz.why: EDTA is a potassium salt that also chelates calcium, so carryover produces exactly this paired pattern: high potassium with low calcium. True renal hyperkalemia does not characteristically drop calcium this way, and citrate fill and tourniquet timing affect other analytes.

quiz.q: A light blue citrate tube arrives at the lab filled to about 60% of the line. What result does this produce?
choices: A falsely shortened PT and aPTT
A falsely elevated potassium
A falsely prolonged PT and aPTT, and the specimen is rejected
No effect; the lab corrects for volume
quiz.why: The citrate volume is fixed for a 9:1 ratio with a full tube, so underfilling leaves excess anticoagulant that binds extra calcium and prolongs clotting times. Shortened times come from heparin or clot activator carryover instead.

quiz.q: Which tube is used for a CBC with differential?
choices: Gold SST
Light blue
Gray
Lavender EDTA
quiz.why: Lavender K2 EDTA preserves cell morphology for counting. Gold SST is for serum chemistries, light blue for coagulation, and gray with fluoride and oxalate for glucose, lactate and alcohol.

quiz.q: How should an EDTA tube be mixed after collection?
choices: Inverted gently end over end 8 to 10 times
Shaken briskly for 5 seconds
Inverted 3 times
Not mixed; the additive dissolves on its own
quiz.why: Eight to ten complete gentle inversions distribute the anticoagulant without shearing cells. Shaking hemolyzes the sample, three inversions is the citrate rule, and inadequate mixing lets the tube clot and become unrunnable.

quiz.q: Which antecubital vein carries the highest risk of nerve injury and arterial puncture?
choices: Median cubital
Cephalic
Basilic
Dorsal metacarpal
quiz.why: The brachial artery and median nerve run directly beneath the basilic vein, making it the last choice in the antecubital fossa. The median cubital is well anchored with no major structures under it, and the cephalic is the second choice.

quiz.q: A tourniquet has been in place for four minutes while you search for a vein. What analytes are most affected if you draw now?
choices: Potassium, calcium, total protein and hematocrit all falsely high from hemoconcentration
Glucose falsely low only
PT and aPTT falsely shortened
White blood cell count falsely low
quiz.why: Prolonged venous stasis pushes water out of the vessel, concentrating everything left behind, which raises potassium, calcium, protein and hematocrit. Release the tourniquet, wait about two minutes, and reapply just before puncture.

quiz.q: A patient on warfarin has just had blood drawn from the antecubital fossa. How is the site managed?
choices: Bend the elbow over the gauze for 2 minutes
Apply a bandage and release the patient immediately
Hold firm direct pressure with the arm straight for 10 minutes or more
Hold pressure for 30 seconds, then tape
quiz.why: Anticoagulated patients need extended direct pressure, 10 minutes or longer, with the arm straight. Bending the elbow over gauze is a classic cause of hematoma, and a bandage alone does not apply pressure.

quiz.q: Which action during a draw most directly causes a falsely elevated potassium without any hemolysis?
choices: Vigorous fist pumping by the patient
Using a 21 G needle
Releasing the tourniquet before withdrawing
Inverting the tube 8 times
quiz.why: Repeated muscle contraction releases potassium from muscle cells into local blood, raising the measured value independently of cell rupture. A 21 G needle, early tourniquet release and correct inversions are all protective, not harmful.

quiz.q: Which of these most commonly causes hemolysis in an emergency department draw?
choices: Using a 21 G straight needle at the median cubital
Filling the tube to its stated volume
Labeling the tube at the bedside
Drawing blood through an existing IV catheter
quiz.why: Blood pulled through a narrow plastic catheter with turbulence at every junction shears red cells, and it is the single largest driver of ED hemolysis. The other three options are correct technique that reduces hemolysis or is unrelated.

quiz.q: The lab reports a potassium of 6.9 with a note that the specimen was grossly hemolyzed. The patient is alert with no symptoms. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Tell the lab it is spurious and cancel it
Report it to the nurse, then redraw from a fresh venipuncture with a 21 G needle and correct order of draw
Redraw from the same IV line that was used originally
Wait for the morning labs
quiz.why: Reporting comes first because only a clinician decides whether a critical value is real, and the patient is treated as though it might be until disproven. The redraw must eliminate the hemolysis cause, which means a fresh stick rather than the same line.

quiz.q: Which set of results is characteristic of a hemolyzed specimen?
choices: High potassium, high LDH, high AST, low glucose
Low potassium, low LDH, high glucose
High sodium, high chloride, normal potassium
High white count, low platelets
quiz.why: Red cell contents spill into the serum, so intracellular analytes like potassium, LDH, AST, magnesium and phosphate rise while glucose and sodium are diluted or consumed. The other patterns reflect different processes entirely.

quiz.q: Why does the lab reject a specimen marked clotted?
choices: The additive has expired
The tube was not inverted promptly or filled too slowly, so cell counts are inaccurate and the analyzer can be damaged
Too much blood was drawn
It was drawn in the wrong order
quiz.why: Clots form when an anticoagulant tube is mixed late or filled slowly. The cells trapped in the clot are removed from the count, so results are wrong, and clots can obstruct the analyzer. Order of draw and volume cause different rejection reasons.

quiz.q: You are drawing blood cultures with a butterfly set. Which bottle do you inoculate first and why?
choices: Anaerobic, because anaerobes are more fragile
Neither; both are filled simultaneously
Whichever bottle is closer at hand
Aerobic, because the tubing holds about 0.5 mL of air that will enter the first bottle
quiz.why: Butterfly tubing dead space pushes air into the first bottle, and air harms anaerobic recovery, so it goes to the aerobic bottle. The anaerobic-first rule applies to syringe draws, where there is no line air.

quiz.q: What is the correct adult blood culture volume and site arrangement?
choices: 8-10 mL per bottle, two sets from two separate venipuncture sites
5 mL per bottle, both sets from one site
20 mL in a single aerobic bottle
2 mL per bottle, one set
quiz.why: Volume is the strongest predictor of growth, at 8-10 mL per bottle and 20 mL per set, and two separate sites are what make a positive interpretable. One site or low volume produces results that cannot be distinguished from contamination.

quiz.q: Which step most directly reduces blood culture contamination?
choices: Drawing from an existing IV line
Filling the anaerobic bottle first regardless of device
Scrubbing the skin with chlorhexidine for 30 seconds and allowing it to dry fully
Refrigerating the bottles until transport
