quiz.why: Contamination comes from skin flora carried in on the needle, so friction scrubbing and full drying time are what kill them. Line draws have a higher contamination rate, bottle order depends on the device, and cultures are never refrigerated.

quiz.q: A septic patient needs cultures, but the nurse is holding antibiotics at the bedside. What is correct?
choices: Give antibiotics first; timing is everything
Draw the cultures first, as long as doing so does not meaningfully delay the antibiotics
Skip the cultures since antibiotics are starting
Draw cultures one hour after the antibiotics
quiz.why: Antibiotics sterilize the blood within minutes, and cultures drawn afterward may never identify the organism or its sensitivities. Cultures precede the first dose whenever obtaining them does not meaningfully delay it, which is a core part of the hour-1 bundle.

quiz.q: A dehydrated elderly patient has no visible or palpable veins. Which action is most likely to succeed?
choices: Slap the antecubital fossa firmly several times
Use a 25 G needle in a hand vein
Tighten the tourniquet as much as possible
Apply a warm pack for 3 to 5 minutes and let the arm hang dependent
quiz.why: Warmth produces measurable vasodilation and gravity fills the veins. Slapping hemolyzes and bruises, an over-tight tourniquet collapses the vein and hemoconcentrates the sample, and a 25 G needle risks hemolysis.

quiz.q: You have attempted a draw twice without success on a patient who needs a stat lactate. What do you do?
choices: Try a third time on the other arm
Hand off to a more experienced technician or nurse and tell them it is time-critical
Cancel the order and document unable to obtain
Draw from the arm with the infusing IV
quiz.why: The two-attempt rule exists because success falls and harm rises with each further stick by the same person. Handing off preserves the patient and the clock; cancelling abandons a time-critical test, and a line draw above an infusion gives a diluted result.

quiz.q: Which IV catheter is the standard choice for a CT with contrast?
choices: 24 G yellow in the hand
22 G blue in the forearm
18 or 20 G in the antecubital fossa
16 G gray in the wrist
quiz.why: Power injectors deliver contrast at high flow rates, so an 18-20 G in a large proximal vein is the usual requirement. Smaller or more distal catheters can rupture the vein, and the wrist is avoided because of nearby structures.

quiz.q: You get flashback during an IV start and immediately try to advance the catheter, which will not thread. What most likely happened?
choices: The vein is thrombosed
The tourniquet was released too early
The gauge is too large
The catheter tip was still in the vein wall because the unit was not advanced 1-2 mm after flashback
quiz.why: Flashback means the needle tip has entered the lumen, but the catheter tip sits slightly behind it. Lowering the angle and advancing the whole unit 1-2 mm places the catheter inside before it is threaded, and skipping that step is the most common cause of failure.

quiz.q: A patient receiving IV contrast develops a swollen, cool, tight forearm with no blood return. What is the correct action?
choices: Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in place, and notify the nurse and provider immediately
Remove the catheter and apply a warm compress
Flush the line vigorously to clear the obstruction
Slow the infusion and continue
quiz.why: Contrast is a vesicant, making this extravasation with a risk of tissue necrosis. The catheter stays in because it may be needed for aspiration or an antidote, and a clinician decides. Flushing forces more vesicant into tissue.

quiz.q: During an attempted IV start, bright red blood pulses into the chamber under its own pressure. What do you do?
choices: Continue and thread the catheter, then flush
Attach a syringe and draw a blood gas
Remove the device immediately and hold firm pressure for at least 5 to 10 minutes, then notify the nurse and provider
Leave it in place and ask the nurse to assess later
quiz.why: Pulsatile bright red blood filling the chamber under its own pressure is an arterial puncture. Immediate removal with prolonged firm pressure prevents a hematoma or pseudoaneurysm, and it must be reported and documented, not observed later.

quiz.q: A patient in shock with cold, mottled hands has a fingerstick glucose of 42 but is alert and conversational. What should you do?
choices: Treat the hypoglycemia immediately without further testing
Recognize that fingersticks are unreliable in shock and poor perfusion, report it, and obtain a venous or blood gas glucose
Repeat the fingerstick on the same finger
Chart the value and take no further action
quiz.why: Capillary glucose requires a perfused fingertip, so shock, hypothermia and edema make it unreliable in either direction. The value is reported and confirmed by a venous or point-of-care blood gas sample, not dismissed and not acted on blindly.

quiz.q: A urine culture is ordered on a patient with an indwelling Foley catheter. Where does the specimen come from?
choices: The drainage bag
A fresh void into a cup
By disconnecting the catheter from the tubing
The cleaned sampling port on the tubing
quiz.why: Bag urine has been sitting and growing organisms for hours and is uninterpretable for culture. The port is cleaned and aspirated. Disconnecting the closed system introduces infection risk, and a catheterized patient cannot provide a clean void.

quiz.q: You sustain a needlestick from a device used on an unknown-status patient. What is the correct immediate action?
choices: Squeeze the site to express blood, apply bleach, and finish your shift
Wash with soap and water and report immediately so source testing and prophylaxis decisions can start within hours
Report at the end of the shift with an incident form
Do nothing unless the source patient is known to be infected
quiz.why: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective when started within hours and generally within 72 hours, so immediate reporting is clinical care. Squeezing and bleach cause tissue damage without lowering transmission risk, and delay forfeits the treatment window.

scenarios.title: Sepsis workup on a one-hour clock
scenarios.intro: 20:15. Room 6, a 72-year-old man from a nursing facility with fever, a cough and new confusion. Temp 39.1 C, heart rate 118, respiratory rate 26, blood pressure 96/58. The physician has just said: sepsis, probable pneumonia, start the bundle — two sets of cultures, lactate, CBC, chemistry, coags, type and screen, and a line. Antibiotics are being mixed in the medication room right now.

steps.prompt: You are gathering supplies at the cart. The nurse says the antibiotic will be ready in about six minutes.

choices.text: Lay out both culture sets, the tubes in order of draw, chlorhexidine, two butterfly sets and the IV supplies before touching the patient
choices.feedback: Right. The two most common reasons for a repeat stick are a tube you did not bring and a tube you did not fill. Six minutes is plenty if you set up once.

choices.text: Go in with the chemistry tubes now and come back for the culture bottles
choices.feedback: Two trips means two sticks or a needle left in a vein while you walk. Cultures come first in the order of draw, so leaving them behind guarantees a redo.

choices.text: Tell the nurse to hold the antibiotic indefinitely until everything is drawn
choices.feedback: Cultures come before antibiotics only when obtaining them will not meaningfully delay the drug. Six minutes is reasonable; an open-ended hold is not, because antibiotic delay itself raises mortality.

choices.text: Set up for the first culture set and the IV, planning to get the second set right after
choices.feedback: Workable, and better than two trips for tubes. Just be sure the second set is genuinely from a second site and actually happens — a single set leaves the result uninterpretable.

steps.prompt: At the bedside. He tells you his name slowly but correctly and his date of birth matches the band. You have found a good median cubital vein on the right arm and a cephalic on the left forearm. You are using a butterfly for the first culture set.

choices.text: Scrub the bottle septa with alcohol, scrub the skin with chlorhexidine for 30 seconds, let it dry fully, then draw the aerobic bottle first
choices.feedback: Correct on all three. The septum is not sterile under the cap, drying time is what actually kills the skin flora, and with a butterfly the tubing air belongs in the aerobic bottle.

choices.text: Scrub the skin for 30 seconds and stick right away while it is still wet, since time matters
choices.feedback: Drying time is not optional — it is when the antiseptic works. A wet stick raises contamination risk and hemolyzes the sample, and one contaminated culture costs days of unnecessary antibiotics.

choices.text: Use an alcohol wipe alone for 10 seconds and fill the anaerobic bottle first
choices.feedback: Two errors. A brief alcohol wipe does not achieve the required skin antisepsis, and anaerobic-first is the syringe rule; with a butterfly, tubing air belongs in the aerobic bottle.

choices.text: Scrub properly, then re-palpate the vein with a gloved finger just before sticking
choices.feedback: The prep and the instinct to confirm are both reasonable, but re-touching prepped skin recontaminates it. Palpate above the prepped area, or re-prep, or mark the spot mentally before you scrub.

steps.prompt: First set is in, roughly 9 mL per bottle. You still need the second culture set from a different site and all the other tubes: lactate, CBC, chemistry, coags, and a type and screen.

choices.text: Draw the second culture set from the left forearm at a separate prepped site, then on that same stick fill light blue, gold, lavender and pink in that order
choices.feedback: Correct. Second site makes the cultures interpretable, and the order is cultures, light blue, gold, green, lavender, gray. Doing it on one stick spares the patient a third needle.

choices.text: Draw the second set from the same right arm site so you do not have to stick him twice
choices.feedback: That defeats the entire point. Two sets from one site cannot distinguish contamination from real bacteremia, and the result becomes uninterpretable no matter what grows.

choices.text: Draw the second set, then fill lavender first so the CBC is not forgotten, and the rest after
choices.feedback: Never. EDTA carryover from the lavender tube falsely raises potassium and lowers calcium in everything drawn after it — the exact artifact that produces a critical potassium in a patient who is fine.

choices.text: Draw the second set at a new site, then send only the lactate and CBC now and come back for the rest
choices.feedback: The second site is right, but splitting the draw means another stick on a septic, hypotensive, hard-to-access patient. Fill everything on the stick you already have.

steps.prompt: 20:26. Everything is drawn. The antibiotic is hanging at the door. You have tubes, culture bottles and an IV that is flushed and secured with a 20 G in the left forearm.

choices.text: Label everything at the bedside with name, date of birth, date, exact time and your initials, note the culture sites, tell the nurse cultures are done, and hand-walk the lactate
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Saying cultures are done is what releases the antibiotic, the site note makes the cultures interpretable later, and lactate is time-sensitive in many labs.

choices.text: Carry the tubes to the counter to label them where there is more room
choices.feedback: Labeling away from the bedside is how specimens from two patients get swapped, and a mislabeled type and screen can cause a fatal transfusion reaction. Label in the room, every time.

choices.text: Send everything by pneumatic tube including the type and screen and the cultures, then tell the nurse
choices.feedback: Check your policy first — blood bank specimens are excluded from the tube system at many hospitals, and tube acceleration can hemolyze samples. Also, the nurse needed to know about the cultures before you left.

choices.text: Label at the bedside, then go tell the nurse the cultures are drawn before doing anything else with the specimens
choices.feedback: Good. Releasing the antibiotic is the highest-value thing you can do at this moment, and the labeled tubes are safe on the counter for the thirty seconds it takes.

steps.prompt: 20:52. The lab calls: the lactate is `4.6 mmol/L`. The nurse is in another room. The patient's repeat pressure just cycled at 88/50 and he is harder to rouse than he was thirty minutes ago.

choices.text: Find the nurse now and say: room 6, lactate 4.6, pressure down to 88/50, more somnolent, respiratory rate 28 — he needs you
choices.feedback: Correct. A lactate of 4 or higher with hypotension is the trigger for `30 mL/kg` of crystalloid in the hour-1 bundle, and a falling mental status is the finding that cannot wait for a callback.

choices.text: Write the lactate on the chart and continue with your next patient
choices.feedback: A critical lactate with worsening hypotension and mentation is not a charting task. The bundle clock and the patient's trajectory both require a clinician at the bedside now.

choices.text: Redraw the lactate first to confirm it before telling anyone
choices.feedback: A repeat lactate is part of the bundle, but it happens after fluids, not instead of reporting. Confirming first delays the intervention the number is supposed to trigger.

choices.text: Recheck a manual blood pressure while calling out to the nurse from the doorway
choices.feedback: Good instinct — a manual confirmation is worth thirty seconds before a treatment decision — as long as the call for the nurse goes out at the same moment rather than after.

scenarios.debrief: Two clocks ran at once in this case, and both were served by preparation rather than speed. The **bundle clock** requires cultures before antibiotics, but only when drawing them does not meaningfully delay the drug — which is why laying out every tube and bottle before entering the room was the decision that made everything else possible. The **technical rules** did not bend for the emergency: bottle septa scrubbed, chlorhexidine given its full 30 seconds and its full drying time, two sets from two separate sites, aerobic first because a butterfly pushes tubing air into the first bottle, and the order of draw held — cultures, light blue, gold, green, lavender, gray — because EDTA carryover would have produced a fake critical potassium in a patient who already had enough real problems. Labels went on at the bedside. And the last step is the one people forget: **telling the nurse the cultures are drawn is what releases the antibiotic.** A perfect draw that nobody knows about is still an antibiotic delay.

scenarios.title: Potassium of 6.8 on a patient who looks fine
scenarios.intro: 11:40. The lab calls the desk with a critical value: potassium `6.8 mmol/L` on room 3, a 45-year-old woman here since 09:30 for a sprained ankle who is now waiting on an orthopedics consult. You drew her basic metabolic panel yourself at 10:05. She is sitting up, on her phone, with no complaints beyond her ankle.

steps.prompt: You are the one holding the phone. The lab technologist is waiting for a read-back.

choices.text: Read the value back to confirm it, ask whether the specimen was hemolyzed, and take it straight to the nurse
choices.feedback: All three, in that order. Read-back is required for critical values, the hemolysis question is free information the lab already has, and the nurse must hear a critical potassium within seconds regardless of what you suspect.

choices.text: Tell the lab it is obviously hemolyzed because the patient is fine, and ask them to cancel it
choices.feedback: You do not get to cancel a critical result, and a patient with a real potassium of 6.8 can look completely well right up until the arrest. Only a clinician makes that call.

choices.text: Note it and mention it when the nurse next comes by
choices.feedback: A critical value has a mandated notification timeframe, usually measured in minutes. Waiting for the nurse to wander past is a documented reporting failure.

choices.text: Read it back, then go redraw immediately before telling anyone
choices.feedback: The redraw is coming, but reporting comes first. If the value is real, the delay costs treatment time, and the nurse may want an ECG before anything else happens.

steps.prompt: The lab says the specimen was flagged as moderately hemolyzed. You tell the nurse, who tells the physician. He says: get me a 12-lead now and redraw the potassium. Then he asks you how the original was drawn.

choices.text: Answer honestly: it was drawn off the 22 G IV start in her hand with a syringe, the tourniquet was on a while, and the tubes were drawn lavender before gold
choices.feedback: That is exactly the information he needs, and it names three separate causes: line draw, prolonged stasis, and EDTA carryover. Honesty here shortens the whole workup.

choices.text: Say you drew it normally and cannot think of anything unusual
choices.feedback: Vagueness leaves the team unable to tell artifact from disease, which usually means more tests, a longer stay, and sometimes treatment the patient did not need. The technique is data.

choices.text: Explain the technique but leave out the tube order because it probably did not matter
choices.feedback: The tube order is the most specific clue of the three. EDTA carryover raises potassium and lowers calcium in a recognizable pattern, and the physician can check the calcium to confirm it.

choices.text: Answer honestly and offer to pull up the original result to see whether the calcium was low
choices.feedback: Good thinking. A high potassium paired with a low calcium points specifically at EDTA carryover rather than hemolysis alone, and it is a two-second check that narrows the question.

steps.prompt: The 12-lead is clean: normal sinus rhythm at 76, no peaked T waves, normal QRS width, P waves present. The physician says: no ECG changes, but a real 6.8 still needs treating, so get me a clean redraw.

choices.text: Fresh venipuncture at the median cubital with a 21 G straight needle, tourniquet under a minute, alcohol fully dry, no fist pumping, correct order of draw, gentle inversions, hand-walked to the lab
choices.feedback: That is the full list, and every item on it addresses a specific cause. This is the draw that answers the question, so it is worth doing slowly and correctly.

choices.text: Redraw from the same hand IV so you do not have to stick her again
choices.feedback: The line draw is the most likely cause of the first result. Repeating it reproduces the artifact and wastes another hour on an uninterpretable answer.

choices.text: Use a 23 G butterfly with a 20 mL syringe to be gentle on her veins
choices.feedback: A large syringe on a small needle generates high shear force and is a classic hemolysis cause — the opposite of gentle. A 21 G straight needle at the median cubital is both kinder and cleaner.

choices.text: Do the clean venipuncture but send it in the pneumatic tube so the result comes faster
choices.feedback: The technique is right, and for a routine chemistry the tube is usually acceptable. But tube acceleration can hemolyze samples, which is the exact artifact you are trying to rule out — hand-walk this one.

steps.prompt: 12:20. The redraw resulted: potassium `4.1 mmol/L`, calcium normal, no hemolysis flag. The nurse asks you to tell her what happened so she can document it and so nobody repeats it.

choices.text: Explain the three causes — line draw, tourniquet time, lavender before gold — and say you will draw her ankle-clinic recheck from a fresh stick in the correct order
choices.feedback: Correct. Naming the specific causes is what prevents the next one, and it turns a near miss into a process fix rather than an embarrassment to bury.

choices.text: Say the first sample must have been a lab error
choices.feedback: It was not a lab error; the lab correctly flagged it as hemolyzed. Blaming the lab hides the real cause and guarantees the same result on the next patient.

choices.text: Say it was just a bad draw and leave it there
choices.feedback: True but useless. Bad draw names no mechanism, so nobody learns what to change. The specific causes are what make the next draw better.

choices.text: Explain the causes and ask whether the department has a policy on drawing labs from a fresh IV start
choices.feedback: Good. Drawing at the moment of a fresh start before fluids run is acceptable in most departments, but drawing off an established line is not, and knowing your own policy is the durable fix.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to remember: **a critical result in a patient who looks well is still reported, still worked up, and never cancelled by the person who drew it.** A real potassium of `6.8` can produce no symptoms at all until it produces an arrest, which is why the ECG came before the redraw — peaked T waves, a widening QRS or a flattening P wave would have made this a treatment emergency in seconds. The artifact side of the case had three separate causes stacked on one specimen: **drawing through an IV catheter** (the largest single source of ED hemolysis), **a tourniquet left on past a minute** (hemoconcentration raises potassium, calcium, protein and hematocrit), and **a lavender tube drawn before the chemistry tube** (EDTA carryover raises potassium and lowers calcium, a pattern you can look for in the original result). The clean redraw is the whole answer: fresh venipuncture, `21 G`, short tourniquet time, dry alcohol, no fist pumping, correct order, gentle inversions, hand-walked. And the last step matters most: naming the specific mechanisms out loud is what stops the same result appearing on the next patient.
